parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Complete Table 1.1 by putting a tick (✓) in the appropriate column to indicate whether the listed quantities are scalars or vectors.

Table 1.1

| quantity | scalar | vector |
| acceleration |  |  |
| density |  |  |
| temperature |  |  |
| momentum |  |  |
hints: Hint 1: Ask yourself for each quantity - does it make sense to give it a direction? If only a size and unit fully describes it, it is a scalar.
Hint 2: Think of the defining equations: $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ and $p = mv$ involve velocity, while $\rho = m/V$ involves only masses and sizes.
parts.proper_answer: acceleration: vector, density: scalar, temperature: scalar, momentum: vector.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what makes a vector different**
Think of sitting with the quantities. A scalar like $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ is complete on its own. A vector like $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to the east is incomplete without the direction. Vectors follow direction rules for adding.

Step 2: **Sort the four quantities**
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so it inherits direction - vector. Momentum is $p = mv$, mass times velocity, so it also has the direction of velocity - vector. Density is mass divided by volume, both directionless - scalar. Temperature is just hotness on a scale - scalar.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Describe qualitatively the motion of the train between time $t = 0$ and time $t = 1.0\text{ s}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at how the steepness of the $d$ against $t$ curve in Fig. 1.1 changes between $t = 0$ and $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ - what does a flattening curve tell you about speed?
parts.proper_answer: The train decelerates (slows down) as the gradient of the distance-time graph decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read speed from steepness**
For a distance-time graph, speed is the gradient. A steep curve means fast, a flat curve means slow. Between $t = 0$ and $t = 1.0\text{ s}$ the curve in Fig. 1.1 starts steep and gets flatter and flatter.

Step 2: **Describe in words**
Flattening means the distance covered per second is getting smaller, so the train is slowing down. That is deceleration. No numbers are needed, just this qualitative trend.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the speed of the train at time $t = 2.0\text{ s}$.
hints: Hint 1: Remember that instantaneous speed at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$ is not $d/t$, it is the steepness of the curve exactly at that point, so you need to imagine a tangent line touching the curve there.
Hint 2: Pick two widely spaced points on your tangent line and divide the rise in $d$ by the run in $t$ to get the gradient in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: speed $\approx 0.24\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from tangent gradient $\Delta d / \Delta t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Draw the tangent at t = 2.0 s**
Place a ruler so it just touches the curve at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$ and follows its slope. The curve is almost straight there, so the tangent follows the curve closely.

Step 2: **Calculate gradient = speed**
Read off two points on the tangent, well apart for accuracy, for example: $$v = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t} \approx \frac{0.56 - 0.20}{3.0 - 1.5} \approx \frac{0.36}{1.5}$$ $$v \approx 0.24\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ Any sensible tangent gives about $0.23$ to $0.25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The straight section of track in (b) is part of the loop of track shown in Fig. 1.2.

{{figure:figure_1_2}}

Fig. 1.2

The train completes exactly one lap of the loop.

State and explain the average velocity of the train over the one complete lap.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the two definitions: average speed uses total distance, but average velocity uses total displacement - where is the train relative to its start after exactly one lap?
parts.proper_answer: Average velocity is zero because total displacement for one complete lap is zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use displacement, not distance**
This is the classic trap. Speed cares about how far the wheels turned. Velocity cares about change in position: $$\text{average velocity} = \frac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}}$$ After exactly one lap of the loop in Fig. 1.2 the train is back where it started, so final position minus initial position is zero. Zero divided by any time is zero, even though the average speed is non-zero.
